title: 3  PAC Learning
text:
3.1 PAC learnability
As we will see below, through the assumptions made above we are not certain of finding the correct predictor that completely nullifies the true error, but we will have the possibility of getting as close as possible. In particular, we will say that the learning is probably approximately correct and in this sense we will speak of PAC learning.
In detail, we mean the following:
On these ideas rests the following fundamental theorem:
Usually in practice one starts from \(m\), which is known, and chooses to increase or decrease the parameters \(\epsilon\) and \(\delta\) to find the best algorithm that fits the data: since \(m\) is inversely proportional to both parameters, as they decrease it is necessary for the number of points in \(\mathcal{S}\) to be larger for the hypotheses of the theorem to be respected, and this is quite obvious if we think about the fact that increasing \(m\) means increasing the representativeness of \(\mathcal{S}\).
The crucial point of the whole theorem is that we know of the existence of “unlucky” learning sets that lead to fallacious functions, since for them the empirical risk (low) is very different from the true error (high); we therefore place an upper limit on the probability of sampling these “deceptive” sets given by the parameter \(\delta\) and we fix a tolerance threshold for the true error through \(\epsilon\). In all this, the proof of the theorem (It is not required for this course and will therefore not be reported.) clarifies that it is the finiteness of the class \(\mathcal{H}\) that guarantees that there is no overfitting with a probability of \(1-\delta\).
The concept of PAC learning is also useful for defining a property related to it, which is that of PAC learnability.
First of all, we generally indicate with \(m_{\mathcal{H}}(\epsilon,\delta)\) a natural number associated with the class \(\mathcal{H}\) called sample complexity; being dependent on the parameters \(\epsilon\) and \(\delta\), which we know go from \(0\) to \(1\), then we can consider \(m_{\mathcal{H}}\) as a function of the type \((0,1)^2\to\mathbb{N}\).
At this point we can make the property explicit as follows:
The other side of the coin of this definition is that there are certainly hypothesis classes that are not PAC learnable: for such hypotheses, therefore, there will always be the possibility of having an overfitting of the data, regardless of how large the learning set is chosen.
PAC learnability therefore guarantees the possibility of approaching with a certain confidence an algorithm with a true error close to zero, provided that the size of \(\mathcal{S}\) is increased.
From the theorem on PAC learning and the definition of PAC learnability, an obvious corollary follows:
It should be borne in mind that the one just written is a sufficient but not necessary condition, in the sense that there are hypothesis classes that do not respect the condition (eq:pac-learning-corollario?) but which are still PAC learnable.

title: 3  PAC Learning
text:
A hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$ is **PAC learnable** if there exists a function \hbox{$m_{\mathcal{H}}:(0,1)^2\to\mathbb{N}$} and a learning algorithm with the following property:




    - for every $\epsilon,\delta\in(0,1)$
    - for every distribution $\mathcal{D}$ on $\mathcal{X}$
    - for every prediction rule $f:x\to\{0,1\}$
    - if the **realizability assumption** is valid with respect to $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathcal{D}$ and $f$


then when the learning algorithm is run on $m\geqslant m_{\mathcal{H}}(\epsilon,\delta)$ i.i.d. points according to $\mathcal{D}$ and labeled according to $f$ it returns a hypothesis $h$ such that

$$
    L_{\mathcal{D},f}(h)\leqslant\epsilon
$$

with a probability of *at least* $1-\delta$.





Every **finite** hypothesis class is PAC learnable with sample complexity

$$
    m_{\mathcal{H}}(\epsilon,\delta)\leqslant\frac{\log\left(\frac{\abs{\mathcal{H}}}{\delta}\right)}{\epsilon}
$$

title: 3  PAC Learning
text:
3.2 A more general learning model
All the conditions that we have imposed so far are very stringent and make the applicability of the methods described above in the real world difficult.
A first constraint that can be abandoned is that of the narrowness of the hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\): after all, the corollary on PAC learning tells us that if the class is finite then, that condition being valid, it is certainly PAC learnable; but, in addition to the existence of the possibility of finite classes for which (eq:pac-learning-corollario?) is not respected but which are still PAC learnable, there is also the possibility of infinite classes that are equally PAC learnable.
The two most important limitations assumed to be valid so far, however, are the following:

Realizability assumption
We have assumed that the correct prediction rule is in the considered hypothesis class, that is:
\[
      \exists h^*\in\mathcal{H}:\mathbb{P}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[h^*(x)=f(x)\right]=1
  \]
In practice, this condition is rarely met. Moreover, it would be more realistic to assume that the prediction rule \(f\) does not uniquely determine the labels, because we must consider the presence of sources of noise that can alter the categorization of elements of the domain that are the same.
For these reasons, the prediction rule \(f\) is usually replaced with a joint distribution \(\mathcal{D}\) with respect to the set \(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\) composed essentially of two parts:
  - $\mathcal{D}_x$: the **marginal distribution** that replaces the previous distribution $\mathcal{D}$
  - $\mathcal{D}((x,y)|x)$: the **conditional distribution** that associates to each point $x$ of the domain the probability that it is labeled in one way or another
To give a practical example: to train an algorithm to identify photos of men or women, we could include among the parameters the fact that the subject wears a skirt or not; according to Western norms, skirts are generally worn by women, but there is still a small probability that it is instead worn by a man (think of the Scottish kilt).
Binary classification
So far we have limited ourselves to a set \(\mathcal{Y}\) of the type \(\{0,1\}\), but in many problems it is useful to classify through a larger number of labels. In the case of regression, the dimension of \(\mathcal{Y}\) becomes infinite, as it is necessary to identify a line that fits the points in a space and therefore depends on real parameters.

title: 3  PAC Learning
text:
3.3 Generalization of errors
Let’s proceed by first giving up the realizability assumption, and only later will we also assume a classification that is not necessarily binary.
By extending the concept of a prediction rule, from a function that maps points from \(\mathcal{X}\) to \(\mathcal{Y}\) to a joint distribution on \(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\), it is necessary to redefine the true error.
First of all, we will not have a point \(x\) extracted from \(\mathcal{D}\) but a pair \((x,y)\) extracted from the joint distribution \(\mathcal{D}\), just as we will not have the image \(f(x)\) but we will have to make explicit reference to the element \(y\) belonging to the set \(\mathcal{Y}\). We will therefore rewrite equation (eq:modelli-di-machine-learning-true-error-1?) as:
\[
    \boxed{L_{\mathcal{D}}(h)=\mathcal{D}((x,y):h(x)\neq y)=\mathbb{P}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}}[h(x)\neq y]}
\]
According to what we have said, it will never be possible to have a true error equal to zero, because the prediction rule is not deterministic but probabilistic, so there is a sort of “intrinsic error” that cannot be eliminated even if the “correct” predictor were chosen.
The empirical risk, on the other hand, does not change in its definition (equation (eq:modelli-di-machine-learning-empirical-risk?)), because it refers to the training set \(\mathcal{S}\) which has remained unchanged; let’s just remember that it is the probability that, taking a pair \(\left(x_i,y_i\right)\) randomly (uniform distribution), we have \(h\left(x_i\right)\neq y_i\).

3.3.1 Bayes Optimal Predictor
Our goal is always to find a function \(h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}\) that minimizes \(L_{\mathcal{D}}(h)\).
According to Bayesian statistics, given the distribution \(\mathcal{D}\) on the set \(\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\), the best predictor is the Bayes Optimal Predictor:
\[
    f_{\mathcal{D}}(x)=
    \begin{cases}
        1 \ \ \ \text{if $\mathcal{P}[y=1|x]\geqslant\frac{1}{2}$}\\
        0 \ \ \ \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases}
\]
Its meaning is quite intuitive: given \(x\), if the probability that \(y=1\) is greater than \(\frac{1}{2}\), then it is statistically more likely to be correct in stating that \(y=1\) than the contrary. Rigorously, it is possible to show that \(L_{\mathcal{D}}\left(f_{\mathcal{D}}\right)\leqslant L_{\mathcal{D}}(g)\) for any \(g:\mathcal{X}\to\{0,1\}\).
This algorithm, however, is not applicable in machine learning, because it requires knowledge of the distribution \(\mathcal{D}\) which, on the contrary, is not known.


3.3.2 Agnostic PAC learnability
Even if we give up the idea of looking for the optimal predictor with a loss function equal to zero, we still want to arrive at a function that is quite close to it, and therefore reduce the true error knowing that we can only get close to zero. We can then extend the concept of PAC learnability to that of agnostic PAC learnability as follows:

A hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$ is **agnostic PAC learnable** if there exists a function $m_{\mathcal{H}}:(0,1)^2\to\mathbb{N}$ and a learning algorithm with the following property:




    - for every $\epsilon,\delta\in(0,1)$
    - for every distribution $\mathcal{D}$ on $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}$


then when the learning algorithm is run on $m\geqslant m_{\mathcal{H}}(\epsilon,\delta)$ i.i.d. points according to $\mathcal{D}$ it returns a hypothesis $h$ such that

$$
    L_{\mathcal{D}}(h)\leqslant \min_{h'\in\mathcal{H}}L_{\mathcal{D}}\left(h'\right)+\epsilon
$$

with a probability of *at least* $1-\delta$.

In this way we try to get closer to the minimum error value, which is given by a predictor \(h'\) known only if the distribution \(\mathcal{D}\) is also known.
The most relevant fact is that the realizability assumption is not required for \(\mathcal{H}\), and if it were satisfied then the smallest true error would be zero and we would fall back into the case of classical PAC learnability.

title: 3  PAC Learning
text:
3.4 New types of classification
The second and last assumption that remains to be dropped is that of binary classification; let’s see two other types of classification:

Multiclass classification
The natural extension with respect to the binary one is the multiclass, in which the dimension of \(\mathcal{Y}=\{0,1,\dots,K-1\}\) is \(K>2\). In this case we will not limit ourselves to the classification of images of dogs and cats, but we will also look at birds, fish and so on.
The true error can be defined in the same way, that is, equal to \(0\) if the prediction is correct and \(1\) if it is wrong. The novelty is that we can “play” with the loss function by establishing that there are relative errors that are “less serious” than others: returning to the example mentioned above, we could state that mistaking a dog for a cat is not as wrong as mistaking a dog for a fish.
Regression
Here we further extremize the extension by finding \(\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}\); the dimension of the set of labels is therefore not only infinite but also non-numerable, and for this reason we will no longer indicate \(\mathcal{Y}\) with set of labels but with target set.
In this case it will be inevitable to change the definition of the loss function, because from probability theory we know that, given a probability density function, the probability of being exactly at any point on the real line is zero. We will then see an extension of the definition of the loss function below.


3.4.1 Generalized loss function
Let’s consider the hypothesis class \(\mathcal{H}\), whose elements are the predictors \(h\), and the domain \(\mathcal{Z}=\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\) whose elements are the pairs \((x,y)\).
A loss function in general is defined as a function of the type
\[
    l:\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}_+
\]
The error will therefore be any positive real number determined from a function of \(h\) and \(z\).
From the function just written, a risk function is defined from the expected value of the loss function with \(z\) extracted from the distribution \(\mathcal{D}\):
\[
    \boxed{L_{\mathcal{D}}(h)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathcal{D}}[l(h,z)]}
\]
Similarly, we can redefine the empirical risk as the expected value of the loss given a learning set \(\mathcal{S}=\left(z_1,\dots,z_m\right)\):
\[
    \boxed{L_{\mathcal{S}}(h)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^ml\left(h,z_i\right)}
\]
Let’s see below the simplest loss functions: (The functions indicated with the term objective* are such because in the literature loss functions are translated as objective functions.)*

0-1 objective: used in the case of binary classification and often also of multiclass classification
\[
      l_{0-1}(h,(x,y))=
      \begin{cases}
          0 \ \ \ \text{if $h(x)=y$}\\
          1 \ \ \ \text{if $h(x)\neq y$}
      \end{cases}
  \]
Quadratic objective: used in the case of regression, it penalizes a few large errors
\[
      l_{sq}(h,(x,y))=(h(x)-y)^2
  \]
Mean absolute error: used in the case of regression, it penalizes many small errors
\[
      l_{abs}(h,(x,y))=\abs{h(x)-y}
  \]



3.4.2 Relevance of errors
Sometimes the weight associated with errors depends on the type of application in which an algorithm is used.
Let’s look at a practical example: a fingerprint scanner that has to understand if a fingerprint belongs to its internal register; if this occurs then the user is authorized to access, while if this is not the case the user is not authorized to access and is rejected.
In this problem the classification is binary: in particular we indicate with \(-1\) the rejection and with \(1\) the approval. There will be two types of error: a false approval, when an unauthorized malicious person still manages to access the service, and a false rejection, when an authorized user is rejected.
In general we can build a matrix (It is not called in any particular way by either the professor or the book, but searching on the internet it could be what is called a confusion matrix.) associated with the errors as follows:

According to what is written, the two types of errors have the same weight and contribute in the same way, but it is possible to vary the two weights in order to make one error more “serious” than the other; let’s see two examples.

The discount at the supermarket
We are in 2032: the World Cup is being played in Saudi Arabia, Ferrari has already abandoned the current car to concentrate on the one for 2033 and China has now completely conquered Italy by proposing its supermarkets with fingerprint recognition for possible discounts to those who, in one way or another, favor the Asian regime.
In a case of error, a customer whose fingerprint is registered in the database is rejected, thus not being able to take advantage of the discount to which he is entitled. This, on the whole, is considered more serious than the other type of error, that is, a malicious person who manages to take advantage of the discount through a fingerprint despite not being registered, because in the latter case the store loses a small profit, while in the other it loses a customer who will no longer buy from that supermarket (and will not favor the colonization work of the dragon).

3.4.3 Generalized agnostic PAC learnability
Having now also freed ourselves from binary classification, we can finally define an even more general PAC learnability that allows us to adapt to as many problems as we face in the real world.

A hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$ is **agnostic PAC learnable** with respect to a set $\mathcal{Z}$ and a loss function $l:\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}_+$ if there exists a function $m_{\mathcal{H}}:(0,1)^2\to\mathbb{N}$ and a learning algorithm with the following property:




    - for every $\epsilon,\delta\in(0,1)$
    - for every distribution $\mathcal{D}$ on $\mathcal{Z}$


then when the learning algorithm is run on $m\geqslant m_{\mathcal{H}}(\epsilon,\delta)$ i.i.d. points according to $\mathcal{D}$ it returns a hypothesis $h$ such that

$$
    L_{\mathcal{D}}(h)\leqslant \min_{h'\in\mathcal{H}}L_{\mathcal{D}}\left(h'\right)+\epsilon
$$

with a probability of *at least* $1-\delta$ and with $L_{\mathcal{D}}(h)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\mathcal{D}}[l(h,z)]$.

19.1 Polynomial Classification on Signal to Noise Ratios
In this notebook we are going to explore the use of polynomial classification with polynomial regression. We are going to use the Numpy polyfit function, which performs polynomial regression.
Our use case is a communication problem: we have a set of measurements of the Signal to Noise Ratio (SNR), i.e., the quality of the communication link, in various positions. The SNR depends on two components: firstly, the noise level (which is a random variable that does not depend on position) and the signal attenuation (usually modeled as a polynomial function of the distance).
Our transmitter is in (0,0), and coordinates are in meters. In urban scenarios, the attenuation usually follows a third-degree polynomial, but it might be a fourth- or fifth-degree polynomial in more complex cases. How do we choose between different degrees? We will try with a maximum of 6

def k_fold_cross_validation(x_train: np.ndarray, y_train: np.ndarray, k: int, max_degree: int) -> tuple[tuple, tuple]:
    # The two returned values are the best degree and the list of results for all degrees up to max_degree.
    # The points should be selected randomly.
    # The inputs and labels are already in terms of distance and SNR

    best = -1
    best_perf = 1e20
    results = []

    # Divide training set in K folds
    x_folds = []
    y_folds = []
    fold_points = int(np.floor(len(x_train) / k))
    idx = list(range(len(x_train)))
    for i in range(k):
        fold_idx = random.sample(idx, fold_points)
        idx = [i for i in idx if i not in fold_idx]
        x_folds.append(x_train[fold_idx])
        y_folds.append(y_train[fold_idx])
    # Train and validate
    for deg in range(max_degree + 1):
        degree_perf = 0
        for test in range(k):
            x_train_fold = [x for i, x in enumerate(x_folds) if i != test]
            y_train_fold = [x for i, x in enumerate(y_folds) if i != test]
            x_train_fold = np.concatenate(x_train_fold)
            y_train_fold = np.concatenate(y_train_fold)
            x_validate_fold = x_folds[test]
            y_validate_fold = y_folds[test]
            k_model = fit(x_train_fold, y_train_fold, deg)
            degree_perf += evaluate(x_validate_fold, y_validate_fold, k_model)
        degree_perf /= k
        results.append(degree_perf)
        if (best_perf > degree_perf):
            best = fit(x_train, y_train, deg)
            best_perf = degree_perf

    return best, results

Show code
def k_fold_cross_validation(x_train: np.ndarray, y_train: np.ndarray, k: int, max_degree: int) -> tuple[tuple, tuple]:
    # Fold assignment is vectorised with np.random.permutation reshaped to (k, fold_points):
    # row i is the index list of fold i. The "all folds except i" mask is a boolean
    # of shape (k,) used to gather training rows in O(k) instead of O(k^2) list comps.
    # The inner polyfit/evaluate loop over degrees is intrinsically sequential
    # (np.polyfit doesn't accept a batched degree), so it stays as a for loop.
    n = len(x_train)
    fold_points = n // k
    perm = np.random.permutation(n)[:k * fold_points].reshape(k, fold_points)  # shape (k, fold_points)

    best = -1
    best_perf = 1e20
    results = []
    fold_mask = np.ones(k, dtype=bool)

    for deg in range(max_degree + 1):
        degree_perf = 0.0
        for test in range(k):
            fold_mask[:] = True
            fold_mask[test] = False
            train_idx = perm[fold_mask].ravel()       # shape ((k-1)*fold_points,)
            val_idx = perm[test]                       # shape (fold_points,)
            k_model = fit(x_train[train_idx], y_train[train_idx], deg)

        results.append(degree_perf)
        if best_perf > degree_perf:
            best = fit(x_train, y_train, deg)
            best_perf = degree_perf

    return best, results

def evaluate_tikhonov(x_train: np.ndarray, y_train: np.ndarray, lambda_par: float, max_degree: int) -> tuple[tuple, tuple]:
    results = []
    best = -1
    best_perf = 1e9
    for deg in range(max_degree + 1):

def load_mnist(path: str, kind: str = 'train') -> tp.Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    # Define the path to the data
    labels_path = os.path.join(path, 'K%s-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz' % kind)
    images_path = os.path.join(path, 'K%s-images-idx3-ubyte.gz' % kind)

    # Load the data into numpy arrays (from the gzip files)
    with gzip.open(labels_path, 'rb') as lbpath:
        labels = np.frombuffer(lbpath.read(), dtype=np.uint8,offset=8)
    with gzip.open(images_path, 'rb') as imgpath:
        images = np.frombuffer(imgpath.read(), dtype=np.uint8,offset=16).reshape(len(labels), 784)

    return images, labels

def param_count(hl_size: int, x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> int:
    tot = 0
    input_size, output_size = x.shape[1], len(y)
    tot += (input_size+1)*hl_size[0]
    for i in range(1,len(hl_size)):
        tot += (hl_size[i-1]+1)*hl_size[i]
    tot += (hl_size[-1]+1)*output_size

Define the Activation class that implements the activation functions and the correspondent derivative. In particular, implement the following activation functions: ReLu, Sigmoid.

class Activation:
    """
    Activation function class
    """

    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        """
        Constructor for the Activation class.
        Given a string name, it sets the activation function (and derivative) to be used.
        Args:
            name (str): the name of the activation function to be used.
        """

        self.name = name

    def __call__(self, x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Given an input x, it computes the corresponding activation function.
        \nArgs:
            x (np.ndarray): the input to the activation function.
        \nReturns:
            np.ndarray: the output of the activation function and the input x (used for backpropagation).
        """

        if self.name == 'relu':
            # TODO: Implement the ReLU activation function (replace pass with your code)
            u = np.maximum(0, x)
            return u, x

        elif self.name == 'sigmoid':
            # TODO: Implement the Sigmoid activation function (replace pass with your code)
            u = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))
            return u, x
        else:
            raise ValueError('Activation function not supported')

class Activation:
    """
    Activation function class — fully vectorised implementation.
    Every operation below is already a NumPy element-wise op,
    so it broadcasts naturally over any-shape tensors x (e.g. (n_units, batch_size)).
    """

    def __init__(self, name: str) -> None:
        self.name = name

    def __call__(self, x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        # x: arbitrary shape (typically (n_units, batch_size))   ->   u: same shape
        if self.name == 'relu':
            # ReLU: element-wise max with 0, vectorised over the entire tensor
            u = np.maximum(0.0, x)
            return u, x
        elif self.name == 'sigmoid':
            # Numerically stable sigmoid: avoids overflow for large negative x
            # x: (n_units, batch_size)   ->   u: (n_units, batch_size)
            pos = x >= 0
            u = np.empty_like(x, dtype=np.float64)
            u[pos] = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-x[pos]))
            ex = np.exp(x[~pos])
            u[~pos] = ex / (1.0 + ex)
            return u, x
        else:
            raise ValueError('Activation function not supported')

    def derivative(self, x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        # x: (n_units, batch_size)   ->   d: (n_units, batch_size)
        if self.name == 'relu':
            # Vectorised indicator (x > 0); cast to float for downstream multiplication
            return (x > 0).astype(x.dtype if np.issubdtype(x.dtype, np.floating) else np.float64)
        elif self.name == 'sigmoid':
            # sigma'(x) = sigma(x) * (1 - sigma(x)); reuses the stable sigmoid above
            s, _ = Activation('sigmoid').__call__(x)
            return s * (1.0 - s)
        else:
            raise ValueError('Activation function not supported')

class DiyMlp:
    """
    A Multi-layer Perceptron implementation.
    keep in mind that all the input are considered with the batch_size as the last dimension.
    """

    def __init__(self, layers: list, learning_rate: float):
        """
        Constructor for the DiyMlp class.
        Given a list of layers and a learning rate, it initializes the parameters of the MLP.
        Each layer a part from the last one use as activation function the ReLU, while the last one uses the sigmoid.
        \nArgs:
            layers (list): a list of layers, each element of the list contains the number of neurons of the layer,
            learning_rate (float): the learning rate used during training
        """

        self.n_layers = len(layers)  # number of layers
        params = {}  # dictionary containing the parameters W and b of each layer

        # For each layer, we define the weight matrix W, the bias vector b and the activation function
        for l in range(1, self.n_layers):
            params[f"W{l}"] = np.random.randn(layers[l], layers[l-1]) * 0.01  # initialize the weight matrix of the layer to a normal distribution rescaled by 0.01
            params[f"b{l}"] = np.zeros((layers[l], 1))  # initialize the bias vector of the layer to zeros
            params[f"activation{l}"] = Activation("relu" if l < self.n_layers - 1 else "sigmoid")  # define the activation function of the layer

        self.params = params  # save the parameters of the network
        self.lr = learning_rate  # save the learning rate

    @staticmethod
    def one_hot(x: np.ndarray, n_classes: int) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        It converts the input x into a one-hot encoding.
        \nArgs:
            x (np.ndarray): the input vector containing the labels of the samples.
            n_classes (int): the number of classes.
        \nReturns:
            np.ndarray: the one-hot encoding of x.
        """

        return np.eye(n_classes)[x.reshape(-1)]

    def forward(self, x: np.ndarray) -> tp.Tuple[np.ndarray, list]:
        """
        Implement the forward propagation of the network. For each layer a part the last one, it computes the linear transformation and applies the activation function.
        Given an input x, it computes the forward pass of the network.
        \nArgs:
            x (np.ndarray): the input to the network.
        \nReturns:
            np.ndarray: the output of the network.
            list: a list containing the linear and activation caches.
        """

        caches = []  # list for storing the linear and activation caches

        out = None  # output of the layer

        # For each layer of the model a part the last one ...
        for l in range(1, self.n_layers):
            prev = cp(x) if l == 1 else out  # storing the input of the layer, i.e., the output of the previous layer

            # Linear Hypothesis
            # TODO: Compute the linear hypothesis z = W*a_prev + b (replace None with your code)
            z = np.dot(self.params[f"W{l}"], prev) + self.params[f"b{l}"]

            # Storing the linear cache for backpropagation = (a_prev, W, b)
            # TODO: Store the linear cache (replace None with your code)
            linear_cache = (prev, self.params[f"W{l}"], self.params[f"b{l}"])

            # Applying the activation function on linear hypothesis
            # TODO: Compute the activation function on z (replace None with your code)
            out, activation_cache = self.params[f"activation{l}"](z)

            # storing both the linear and activation cache
            caches.append((linear_cache, activation_cache))

        return out, caches

    @staticmethod
    def cost_function(out: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Given the output of the network out and the ground truth labels y, it computes the cost function (loss).
        This implementation uses the cross-entropy loss.
        \nArgs:
            out (np.ndarray): the output of the network.
            y (np.ndarray): the ground truth labels.
        \nReturns:
            np.ndarray: the cost value.
        """

        return (-1/y.shape[1]) * (np.dot(np.log(out), y.T) + np.dot(np.log(1-out), 1-y.T))

    @staticmethod
    def one_layer_backward(d_pred: np.ndarray, cache: tp.List[tp.Tuple[np.ndarray]], derivative_activation: Activation.derivative) -> tuple:
        """
        Given the derivative of the loss with respect to the output of the layer d_pred and the linear and activation cache,
        it computes the derivative of the loss with respect to the input of the layer d_pred_prev, the derivative of the loss
        with respect to the weights d_w and the derivative of the loss with respect to the bias d_b.
        \nArgs:
            d_pred (np.ndarray): the derivative of the loss with respect to the output of the layer.
            cache (list): a list containing the linear and activation cache.
            derivative_activation (Activation.derivative): the derivative of the activation function.
        \nReturns:
            tuple: a tuple containing the derivative of the loss with respect to the input of the layer dA_prev,
            the derivative of the loss with respect to the weights dW and the derivative of the loss with respect to the bias db.
        """

        linear_cache, activation_cache = cache  # retrieve the linear and activation cache

        z = activation_cache
        d_z = d_pred * derivative_activation(z) # compute the derivative of the loss with respect to z

        pred_prev, w, _ = linear_cache  # retrieve the input of the layer and the weights from the cache
        m = pred_prev.shape[1]  # retrieve the number of samples

        d_w = (1/m) * np.dot(d_z, pred_prev.T)  # compute the derivative of the loss with respect to w
        d_b = (1/m) * np.sum(d_z, axis=1, keepdims=True)  # compute the derivative of the loss with respect to b
        d_pred_prev = np.dot(w.T, d_z)  # compute the derivative of the loss with respect to the input of the layer

        return d_pred_prev, d_w, d_b

    def backprop(self, pred, labels, caches) -> dict:
        """
        Given the output of the network pred, the ground truth labels y and the caches,
        it computes the backward pass of the network.
        \nArgs:
            pred (np.ndarray): the output of the network.
            labels (np.ndarray): the ground truth labels.
            caches (list): a list containing the linear and activation caches.
        \nReturns:
            dict: a dictionary containing the derivatives of the loss with respect to the parameters of the network.
        """

        grads = {}  # dictionary for storing the gradients
        labels = labels.reshape(pred.shape) # reshape the labels to have the same shape as the output of the network
        caches_len = len(caches)

        # Compute the grad of the last layer
        d_pred = -(np.divide(labels, pred) - np.divide(1-labels, 1-pred))  # compute the derivative of the loss with respect to the output of the network
        current_cache = caches[caches_len - 1]  # retrieve the linear and activation cache of the last layer
        grads[f"d_pred{caches_len - 1}"], grads[f"dW{caches_len}"], grads[f"db{caches_len}"] = self.one_layer_backward(d_pred, current_cache, self.params[f"activation{caches_len}"].derivative)

        # Compute the grad for all the other layers in reverse order
        for l in reversed(range(caches_len - 1)):
            current_cache = caches[l]  # retrieve the linear and activation cache of the layer
            grads[f"d_pred{l}"], grads[f"dW{l + 1}"], grads[f"db{l + 1}"] = self.one_layer_backward(grads[f"d_pred{l + 1}"], current_cache, self.params[f"activation{l + 1}"].derivative)  # compute the derivative of the loss with respect to the output of the next layer

        return grads

    def update_parameters(self, grads: dict) -> None:
        """
        Given the gradients grads,it updates the weight matrix and the bias vector using the stochastic gradient descent.
        \nArgs:
            grads (dict): a dictionary containing the derivatives of the loss with respect to the parameters of the network.
        """

        for l in range(self.n_layers - 1):
            self.params[f"W{l + 1}"] = self.params[f"W{l + 1}"] - self.lr*grads[f"dW{l + 1}"]
            self.params[f"b{l + 1}"] = self.params[f"b{l + 1}"] - self.lr*grads[f"db{l + 1}"]

    def train(self, x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, epochs: int) -> None:
        """
        Given the input x, the ground truth labels y and the number of epochs, it trains the network.
        \nArgs:
            x (np.ndarray): the input to the network.
            y (np.ndarray): the ground truth labels.
            epochs (int): the number of epochs.
        """

        x = x.T  # transpose the input to have the batch size as the first dimension
        y = self.one_hot(y, np.unique(y).shape[0]).T  # one-hot encode the labels and transpose to have the batch size as the first dimension

        cost_history = []  # list for storing the cost at each epoch

        # For each epoch ...
        for _ in range(epochs):
            out, caches = self.forward(x)  # compute the output of the network and retrieve the caches
            cost = self.cost_function(out, y)  # compute the cost
            cost_history.append(cost)  # save the cost
            grads = self.backprop(out, y, caches)  # compute the gradients

            self.update_parameters(grads)  # update the parameters of the network using the gradients

    def predict(self, x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        """
        Given the input x, it computes the output of the network.
        \nArgs:
            x (np.ndarray): the input to the network.
        \nReturns:
            np.ndarray: the output of the network.
        """

        x = x.T  # transpose the input to have the batch size as the first dimension
        out, _ = self.forward(x)  # compute the output of the network
        predictions = np.argmax(out, axis=0)  # get the predictions

        return predictions

class DiyMlp:
    """
    Vectorised Multi-layer Perceptron — only the `forward` pass changes.
    Everything is already in the (n_units, batch_size) layout: the single matmul
    z = W @ a_prev + b processes the whole batch at once, which is exactly the
    place where matrix multiplication dominates loop-based code.
    """

    def __init__(self, layers: list, learning_rate: float):
        self.n_layers = len(layers)
        params = {}
        for l in range(1, self.n_layers):
            # W{l}: (layers[l], layers[l-1])   b{l}: (layers[l], 1)
            params[f"W{l}"] = np.random.randn(layers[l], layers[l-1]) * 0.01
            params[f"b{l}"] = np.zeros((layers[l], 1))
            params[f"activation{l}"] = Activation("relu" if l < self.n_layers - 1 else "sigmoid")
        self.params = params
        self.lr = learning_rate

    @staticmethod
    def one_hot(x: np.ndarray, n_classes: int) -> np.ndarray:
        return np.eye(n_classes)[x.reshape(-1)]

    def forward(self, x: np.ndarray) -> tp.Tuple[np.ndarray, list]:
        """
        Fully vectorised forward pass.
        Input layout: x: (d_in, batch_size)  — features in rows, samples in columns.
        For each layer l:
            W{l}:   (d_out, d_in)
            a_prev: (d_in,  batch_size)
            b{l}:   (d_out, 1)   broadcast over batch axis
            z:      (d_out, batch_size)   =   W @ a_prev + b
            out:    (d_out, batch_size)   =   sigma(z)
        The same single matmul handles the entire mini-batch — no Python loop
        over samples — which is exactly the speed-up matrix multiplication
        gives over the naive per-sample formulation.
        """
        caches = []
        out = None

        # The loop over LAYERS cannot be removed: each layer's input is the
        # previous layer's output, so the dependency is sequential by definition.
        # The per-sample loop, however, is fully collapsed into a single GEMM.
        for l in range(1, self.n_layers):
            # a_prev: (d_in, batch_size)
            a_prev = x if l == 1 else out

            W = self.params[f"W{l}"]   # (d_out, d_in)
            b = self.params[f"b{l}"]   # (d_out, 1)

            # Single matmul over the whole batch:
            # W @ a_prev: (d_out, d_in) @ (d_in, batch_size) -> (d_out, batch_size)
            # b broadcasts on the batch axis.
            z = W @ a_prev + b         # z: (d_out, batch_size)

            # Cache layout expected by the provided backprop():
            #   linear_cache     = (a_prev, W, b)
            #   activation_cache = z   (the pre-activation, returned by Activation.__call__)
            linear_cache = (a_prev, W, b)

            # sigma is element-wise and already vectorised over (d_out, batch_size)
            out, activation_cache = self.params[f"activation{l}"](z)

            caches.append((linear_cache, activation_cache))

        return out, caches

    @staticmethod
    def cost_function(out: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        return (-1/y.shape[1]) * (np.dot(np.log(out), y.T) + np.dot(np.log(1-out), 1-y.T))

    @staticmethod
    def one_layer_backward(d_pred: np.ndarray, cache, derivative_activation) -> tuple:
        linear_cache, activation_cache = cache
        z = activation_cache
        d_z = d_pred * derivative_activation(z)
        pred_prev, w, _ = linear_cache
        m = pred_prev.shape[1]
        d_w = (1/m) * np.dot(d_z, pred_prev.T)
        d_b = (1/m) * np.sum(d_z, axis=1, keepdims=True)
        d_pred_prev = np.dot(w.T, d_z)
        return d_pred_prev, d_w, d_b

    def backprop(self, pred, labels, caches) -> dict:
        grads = {}
        labels = labels.reshape(pred.shape)
        caches_len = len(caches)
        d_pred = -(np.divide(labels, pred) - np.divide(1-labels, 1-pred))
        current_cache = caches[caches_len - 1]
        grads[f"d_pred{caches_len - 1}"], grads[f"dW{caches_len}"], grads[f"db{caches_len}"] = self.one_layer_backward(
            d_pred, current_cache, self.params[f"activation{caches_len}"].derivative
        )
        for l in reversed(range(caches_len - 1)):
            current_cache = caches[l]
            grads[f"d_pred{l}"], grads[f"dW{l + 1}"], grads[f"db{l + 1}"] = self.one_layer_backward(
                grads[f"d_pred{l + 1}"], current_cache, self.params[f"activation{l + 1}"].derivative
            )
        return grads

    def update_parameters(self, grads: dict) -> None:
        for l in range(self.n_layers - 1):
            self.params[f"W{l + 1}"] = self.params[f"W{l + 1}"] - self.lr*grads[f"dW{l + 1}"]
            self.params[f"b{l + 1}"] = self.params[f"b{l + 1}"] - self.lr*grads[f"db{l + 1}"]

    def train(self, x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, epochs: int) -> None:
        # x: (n, d_in)  ->  (d_in, n)   y: (n,)  ->  one-hot (n_classes, n)
        x = x.T
        y = self.one_hot(y, np.unique(y).shape[0]).T
        cost_history = []
        for _ in range(epochs):
            out, caches = self.forward(x)
            cost = self.cost_function(out, y)
            cost_history.append(cost)
            grads = self.backprop(out, y, caches)
            self.update_parameters(grads)

    def predict(self, x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        # x: (n, d_in)  ->  (d_in, n)   out: (n_classes, n)   predictions: (n,)
        x = x.T
        out, _ = self.forward(x)
        predictions = np.argmax(out, axis=0)
        return predictions

8.1 Affine Function Model
The first family of functions that we will explore is that of linear functions, useful for solving many problems due to their efficiency in the field of statistical learning, as well as for their simplicity in interpreting many results.
As we saw in the first part of the course, two elements are necessary to define a learning model: a class of hypotheses and an algorithm capable of identifying the best predictor.
We will explore three classes of hypotheses:
The algorithms we will explore are also three:
The starting point for finding linear solutions is to use the class of affine functions (In English affine functions.) from which the various classes of hypotheses mentioned above will then be derived.
It is defined as follows:
\[
    \boxed{L_d=\left\{h_{\boldsymbol{w},b}:\boldsymbol{w}\in\mathbb{R}^d,b\in\mathbb{R}\right\}}
\]
Each function in the class is parameterized by a vector \(\boldsymbol{w}\) of dimension \(d\), called the weight vector, and by a scalar \(b\), called the bias; the parameters, therefore, are a total of \(d+1\).
Each function takes a vector \(\boldsymbol{x}\) as input and transforms it as follows:
\[
    \boxed{h_{\boldsymbol{w},b}(\boldsymbol{x})=\sprod{x}{w}+b=\sum_{i=1}^dx_iw_i+b}
\]
Let \(z\) be the output obtained from the affine function, to this will be applied a further function \(\phi\) which will give the final classification.
This function can be of two types, based on the classification of the label:
Ultimately, the mathematical procedure is as follows:
\[
    \boldsymbol{x} \ \overset{L_d}{\longrightarrow} \ z \ \overset{\phi}{\longrightarrow} \ y
\]
The class of hypotheses will be given by the set of compositions \(\phi\circ L_d\).

title: 8  Linear Predictors
text:
In binary classification we choose \(\phi(z)=sign(z)\) so as to have \(\mathcal{Y}=\{-1,1 re\}\)
In regression we choose \(\phi(z)=z\) so as to have \(\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}\)





8.1.1 Geometric Interpretation
To understand concretely what the described procedure consists of, it is useful to observe a simple example with \(d=2\) which, consequently, will be geometrically located on the Cartesian plane.
Given \(\boldsymbol{x} = (x_1, x_2)\) the affine function will return
\[
    h_{\boldsymbol{w},b}(\boldsymbol{x})=\sprod{x}{w}+b=x_1w_1+x_2w_2+b
\]
In the case of regression, the result is clear from here: the one found is the fitting line of the data, whose parameters will change at each iteration of the algorithm in order to find the one whose fitting is the best.
In the case of binary classification, the line (In three dimensions it would be a plane, and in even higher dimensions hyperplanes.) found represents the dividing line between two regions of the plane: one is where the points are labeled \(1\) (\(h_{\boldsymbol{w},b}(\boldsymbol{x})>0\)), the other where they are labeled \(-1\) (\(h_{\boldsymbol{w},b}(\boldsymbol{x})<0\)).
The weight vector therefore has the role of determining the slope of the line, since \(\boldsymbol{w}\) represents the vector orthogonal to the line itself. Given two points \((x_1',x_2')\), \((x_1'',x_2'')\) located on the line, in fact, we will have that
\[
    \begin{cases}
        w_1x_1'+w_2x_2'=-b\\
        w_1x_1''+w_2x_2''=-b
    \end{cases}
\]
and performing the difference member by member will result in:
\[
    w_1\left(x_1'-x_1''\right)+w_2\left(x_2'-x_2''\right)=0
\]
This quantity can also be rewritten as:
\[
    \left(w_1,w_2\right)\cdot\left(x_1'-x_1'',x_2'-x_2''\right)=0
\]
Since the second vector determines nothing other than the direction of the line, then it is clear that \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is the vector orthogonal to the latter, since their dot product is zero.
The scalar term \(b\), on the other hand, is proportional to the distance of the line from the origin.


8.1.2 Homogeneous Linear Functions
Considering a vector and a scalar is quite problematic from a notation point of view, because you have to incorporate the two elements separately. One way to overcome this drawback is to use the transformation of homogeneous coordinates, which consists in adding a dimension to the vectors \(\boldsymbol{x}\) and \(\boldsymbol{w}\) in the following way:
\[\begin{align*}
    &\boldsymbol{x} \ \longrightarrow \ \boldsymbol{x'}=\left(1,x_1,\dots,x_d\right)\\
    &\boldsymbol{w} \ \longrightarrow \ \boldsymbol{w'}=\left(b,w_1,\dots,w_d\right)
\end{align*}\]
The dot product between the two new vectors will give:
\[
    \sprod{x'}{w'}=b+x_1w_1+\dotsc+x_dw_d=\sum_{i=1}^dx_iw_i+b=\sprod{x}{w}+b
\]
From now on, therefore, we will rewrite the affine functions in the form
\[
    \boxed{h_{\boldsymbol{w},b}(\boldsymbol{x})=\sprod{x'}{w'}=\sum_{i=1}^{d+1}x_i'w_i'}
\]
Through this transformation we have managed to make the affine functions into real linear functions, determined by a single vector of dimension \(d+1\).

text:
8.2 Halfspaces
By choosing binary classification, and therefore \(\phi(z)=sign(z)\), we obtain the class of halfspaces, so called precisely because they divide the considered \(d\)-dimensional space into two halves:
\[
    HS_d=\{x\rightarrow sign\left(\sprod{x'}{w'}\right), \boldsymbol{w'}\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\}
\]
As is predictable, being a binary classification, the loss function is a \(0-1\) objective function.
The realizability condition for this class coincides with linear separability: if the problem is linearly separable then there is at least one halfspace in the class capable of correctly classifying all the points in the space.

8.2.1 Linear Programming
In linear programming, the objective is to maximize a linear function that is subject to constraints:
\[
    \max_{\boldsymbol{w}\in\mathbb{R}^d}\sprod{u}{w} \ \ \text{with} \ A\boldsymbol{w}\geqslant\boldsymbol{v}
\]
where \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}\) is a given matrix, \(\boldsymbol{u}\in\mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\boldsymbol{v}\in\mathbb{R}^m\) are two given vectors and finally \(\boldsymbol{w}\in\mathbb{R}^d\) is the unknown vector to be identified.
This type of problem, called a linear program, can be solved through specific algorithms such as the simplex algorithm, which we do not deal with since it concerns the field of optimization and not machine learning.
What interests us, in fact, is that the empirical risk minimization related to halfspaces can be expressed as a linear program if the realizability assumption is satisfied. To understand how, let’s write the classification of a training set \(\mathcal{S}=\left\{\left(\boldsymbol{x_i},y_i\right)\right\}\) of size \(m\) through halfspaces:
\[
    sign\left(\sprod{x_i}{w}\right)=y_i \ \\
\forall i=1,\dots,m
\]
where, we recall, the first coordinate of \(\boldsymbol{x_i}\) is \(1\) and the first coordinate of \(\boldsymbol{w}\) is the parameter \(b\).
Equivalently, this classification can be rewritten as:
\[
    y_i\sprod{x_i}{w}>0 \ \\
\forall i=1,\dots,m
\]
since the two quantities must have the same sign.
Since the realizability condition is satisfied, there certainly exists a vector \(\boldsymbol{w'}\) such that the classification of all points is correct. We define the vector \(\boldsymbol{w''}\) as follows:
\[
    \boldsymbol{w''}=\frac{\boldsymbol{w'}}{\min\limits_{i\in[1,m]}y_i\sprod{x_i}{w'}}
\]
Substituting in (predictor-lineari-programmazione-lineare-classificazione-halfspace?) we obtain:
\[
    y_i\sprod{x_i}{w''}=\frac{y_i\sprod{x_i}{w'}}{\min\limits_{i\in[1,m]}y_i\sprod{x_i}{w'}}\geqslant1 \ \\
\forall i=1,\dots,m
\]
since the numerator is always greater than or at the limit equal to the denominator.
We have thus shown that there exists a vector \(\boldsymbol{w}\) that satisfies the relation
\[
    y_i\sprod{x_i}{w}\geqslant1 \ \\
\forall i=1,\dots,m
\]
We define the matrix \(A\) as follows: (Each term \(x\) has two indices: the first refers to the element of the training set, and therefore goes from \(1\) to \(m\), while the second refers to the element of the vector, which being in a space of dimension \(d+1\) (we recall that the first element of each vector is a \(1\) added “a posteriori”) will go from \(1\) to \(d+1\).)
\[
    A=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        y_1x_{11} & y_1x_{12} & \dots & y_1x_{1(d+1)}\\
        y_2x_{21} & y_2x_{22} & \dots & y_2x_{2(d+1)}\\
        \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
        y_mx_{m1} & y_mx_{m2} & \dots & y_mx_{m(d+1)}\\
    \end{pmatrix}
\]
Therefore, setting \(\boldsymbol{v}=(1,1,\dots,1)\in\mathbb{R}^m\) we can rewrite (eq:predictor-lineari-programmazione-lineare-classificazione-maggiore-uguale?) as
\[
    A\boldsymbol{w}\geqslant\boldsymbol{v}
\]
that is, the same form of the constraints written in equation (eq:predictor-lineari-programma-lineare?).
The most important difference with respect to a linear program is that the latter requires the maximization of the dot product \(\sprod{u}{w}\) being \(u\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\) a given vector. The point is that according to the ERM algorithm all the vectors that satisfy (eq:predictor-lineari-programmazione-lineare-classificazione-maggiore-uguale?) are equivalent candidates for our hypothesis, since they all nullify the empirical risk; (We will see in the next section how, in reality, it is possible to identify “better” candidates than others through halfspaces.) for this reason, we choose to set \(\boldsymbol{u}\)=(0,0,,0) so that the dot product is the same for all vectors \(\boldsymbol{w}\).


8.2.2 VC Dimension of Halfspaces
We will see below a theorem according to which the VC dimension of homogeneous halfspaces (\(b=0\)) is equal to \(d\). In reality, it is not difficult to guess that for non-homogeneous halfspaces the VC dimension is instead \(d+1\), as a “constraint” related to the passage of the halfspace through the origin is missing.
We can observe some examples that allow us to better understand this discussion. Reasoning on the plane (\(d=2\)) it is easy to see that the VC dimension corresponds to three; given a generic set of three points, in fact, we have:
It would remain to be verified that all sets with four points are not shatterable by any halfspace; referring to figure (fig:predictor-lineari-halfspace-dimensione-vc-d-2-2?) we observe the following:
\item[$@fig:prediction-lineari-halfspace-dimensione-vc-d-2-2-a$] Three points classified in the same way placed at the vertices of an ideal triangle inside which there is the fourth point classified in a different way; it is impossible to isolate the central point in a region of space different from at least one of the vertices.
\item[$@fig:prediction-lineari-halfspace-dimensione-vc-d-2-2-b$] By moving the point to one of the sides of the triangle, the classification according to halfspaces remains impossible.
\item[$@fig:prediction-lineari-halfspace-dimensione-vc-d-2-2-c$] If the point goes outside the triangle then it is possible to classify all the points; let's imagine now, however, to identify a quadrilateral at whose vertices the four points are placed, and that these are classified so that the opposite vertices have the same label which is different from that of the other two: it thus becomes impossible to classify all four points correctly with a halfspace.
Let’s now see the rigorous proof for homogeneous halfspaces.

The VC dimension of the class of homogeneous halfspaces in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is equal to \(**d**\).
- **First part**: $VCdim\left(HS_d\right)\geqslant d$

We just need to verify the existence of a set of points that is shatterable by halfspaces. Let's then consider the simplest one to imagine, that is, the one formed by the canonical basis of the space $\left\{\boldsymbol{e_1},\boldsymbol{e_2},\dots,\boldsymbol{e_d}\right\}$ in which each vector $\boldsymbol{e_i}$ has all null components except for the $i$-th one set to $1$.

The halfspace capable of correctly classifying all the points is the one whose weight vector is

$$
    \boldsymbol{w}=\left(y_1,y_2,\dots,y_d\right)
$$

being $y_i$ the label of the $i$-th point.

In fact, we have

$$
    \sprod{e_i}{w}=y_i \quad \forall i
$$

which certifies the correct classification, and this is valid for any configuration of labels of the points.

- **Second part**: $VCdim\left(HS_d\right)<d+1$

Let's imagine a generic set composed of $d+1$ vectors:

$$
    \left\{\boldsymbol{x_1},\boldsymbol{x_2},\dots,\boldsymbol{x_{d+1}}\right\}
$$

These vectors will certainly not be linearly independent, being in greater number than the dimension of the space. This means, according to linear algebra, that there exists a set of real numbers $\left\{a_1,a_2,\dots,a_{d+1}\right\}$ such that

$$
    \sum_{i=1}^{d+1}a_i\boldsymbol{x_i}=0
$$

Let's now define the following sets:

$$
    I=\left\{i:a_i>0\right\} \ \ \text{and} \ \ J=\left\{j:a_j<0\right\}
$$

At least one of the two is certainly not empty; let's imagine, for now, that neither of them is empty.

In order for @eq:predictor-lineari-dimensione-vc-halfspace-dimostrazione to hold, it is necessary that

$$
    \sum_{i\in I}a_i\boldsymbol{x_i}=\sum_{j\in J}\abs{a_j}\boldsymbol{x_j}
$$

Let's now assume that the set of $d+1$ vectors is *shatterable*; then there exists a weight vector $\boldsymbol{w}$ such that

$$
    \begin{cases}
        \sprod{x_i}{w}>0 & \forall i\in I\\
        \sprod{x_j}{w}<0 & \forall j\in J
    \end{cases}
$$

From which it follows:

$$
    \begin{cases}
        \sum\limits_{i\in I}a_i\sprod{x_i}{w}>0\\
        \sum\limits_{j\in J}\abs{a_i}\sprod{x_j}{w}<0
    \end{cases}
$$

And yet, by the linearity of the dot product, we find that

$$
    \sum\limits_{i\in I}a_i\sprod{x_i}{w}=\sprod{\sum\limits_{i\in I}a_ix_i}{w}
$$

From @eq:predictor-lineari-dimensione-vc-halfspace-dimostrazione-2 it follows:

$$
    \sprod{\sum\limits_{i\in I}a_ix_i}{w}=\sprod{\sum\limits_{j\in J}\abs{a_j}x_j}{w}=\sum\limits_{j\in J}\abs{a_j}\sprod{x_j}{w}
$$

We are thus faced with a contradiction, since the first members of the inequalities of @eq:predictor-lineari-dimensione-vc-halfspace-dimostrazione-3 are equal to each other, when according to the system one is positive and the other is negative. It follows that the set of vectors, in reality, is not shatterable.

In the case where $I$ (or $J$) is empty then the first member (or second member) of @eq:predictor-lineari-dimensione-vc-halfspace-dimostrazione-2 will be null, still maintaining the contradiction given by the last chain of equalities.

title: 8  Linear Predictors
text:
8.3 Perceptron
A linear algorithm that makes explicit use of the class of halfspaces is the perceptron, first introduced by Rosenblatt in 1958 and considered the ancestor of what is a neuron in a neural network.
The objective of the algorithm is to identify a hyperplane (defined by the vector \(\boldsymbol{w}\)) that separates the space in order to correctly classify all the available data.
The method proceeds in steps: we start from a generic vector \(\boldsymbol{w}\) (usually the null vector) and we check the correct classification of the points; once a wrongly labeled point is encountered (we will say misclassified) this will be used to correct \(\boldsymbol{w}\) in order to correctly classify this point; we then repeat the check of all the points, proceeding in the same way until - if the realizability condition is satisfied - all the points will be classified correctly: it is possible to show, in fact, that if the data set is linearly separable then the convergence of the algorithm is guaranteed.
The advantage of the perceptron is that, in most cases, it is a very fast and above all simple algorithm to implement.

8.3.1 Novikoff Perceptron Bound
A fundamental result quantifies the number of mistakes the perceptron makes when learning a linearly separable dataset.

Suppose there exists a weight vector \(\boldsymbol{w}^*\) with \(\|\boldsymbol{w}^*\| = 1\) such that \(y_i \langle \boldsymbol{w}^*, \boldsymbol{x}_i \rangle \geq \gamma\) for all training examples \(i\), where \(\gamma > 0\) is the margin. If \(R = \max_i \|\boldsymbol{x}_i\|\), then the perceptron makes at most \((R/\gamma)^2\) mistakes on any finite training sequence.

This bound shows that the perceptron converges faster when the margin is larger (points are further from the decision boundary) and slower when examples are more distant from the origin. The bound is independent of the dimension of the data, which is a key strength of the perceptron algorithm.


8.3.2 Procedure

The learning set formed by the pairs \(\left(\boldsymbol{x_i},y_i\right)\) is loaded into memory
The vector \(\boldsymbol{w}=(0,\dots,0)\) is initialized, which we will denote by \(\boldsymbol{w^{(1)}}\)
A loop is constructed with \(t=1,2,\dots\) in which, at each iteration, a check is made on the correct classification of all points
 a pair \(\left(\boldsymbol{x_i},y_i\right)\) is identified such that \(y_i\sprod{w^{(t)}}{x_i}\leqslant0\) then we set \(w^{(t+1)}=w^{(t)}+y_ix_i\), otherwise the loop is interrupted and \(w^{(t)}\) is returned

The reason why the weight vector is updated by adding the term \(y_i\boldsymbol{x_i}\) is evident by making the classification check explicit:
\[
    y_i\sprod{w^{(t+1)}}{x_i}=y_i\sprod{w^{(t)}}{x_i}+y_i^2\sprod{x_i}{x_i}=y_i\sprod{w^{(t)}}{x_i}+\norm{\boldsymbol{x_i}}
\]
being \(y_i=\pm1\).
The correction of the vector \(\boldsymbol{w}\), therefore, is made in such a way as to add a certainly positive term, that is, the norm of the vector \(\boldsymbol{x_i}\): if \(\norm{\boldsymbol{x_i}}\geqslant0\) is able to “counterbalance” \(y_i\sprod{w^{(t)}}{x_i}\leqslant0\) then the point \(\boldsymbol{x_i}\) will be correctly classified.
### Theorem on the Convergence of the Method
The only problem left pending is when the algorithm is interrupted. We will see below a theorem that guarantees that, in the case of a linearly separable data set, the perceptron will converge to a solution that correctly classifies all the points; the theorem will also provide us with an upper bound on the number of iterations useful for convergence.

Let $\left(\boldsymbol{x_1},y_1\right),\dots,\left(\boldsymbol{x_m},y_m\right)$ be a linearly separable data set.

We define:


    - $B=\min\left\{\norm{\boldsymbol{w}}:y_i\sprod{w}{x_i}\geqslant1 \ \forall i=1,\dots,m\right\}$
    - $R=\max\norm{\boldsymbol{x_i}}$


Then it follows that:


    - The perceptron stops after *at most* $(RB)^2$ iterations
    - When the perceptron stops, all data are correctly classified

The second thesis is evident from how the perceptron was designed in the first place: as we saw in the procedure, in fact, the moment all the points are classified correctly, the loop is interrupted and so is the algorithm. It therefore remains to be understood how \((RB)^2\) is able to quantify the maximum number of iterations beyond which the perceptron has achieved its purpose, that is, to nullify the empirical risk.

Let:


    - $\boldsymbol{w^*}$ be the weight vector that satisfies the definition of $B$
    - $T$ be the number of iterations followed by the algorithm before it stops


The thesis therefore becomes:

$$
    T\leqslant(RB)^2
$$

Rearranging the terms we get:

$$
    \frac{T}{(RB)^2}\leqslant1 \ \iff \ \frac{\sqrt{T}}{RB}\leqslant1 \ \iff \ \frac{T}{\sqrt{T}RB}\leqslant1
$$

Let's now introduce a last term, that is, the dot product between the vectors $\boldsymbol{w^*}$ and $\boldsymbol{w^{(T+1)}}$ divided by the product of their norms. By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, this term is certainly less than or equal to $1$:

$$
    \frac{\sprod{w^*}{w^{(T+1)}}}{\norm{\boldsymbol{w^*}}\norm{\boldsymbol{w^{(T+1)}}}}\leqslant1
$$

The idea of the proof is to verify that

$$
    \frac{T}{\sqrt{T}RB}\leqslant\frac{\sprod{w^*}{w^{(T+1)}}}{\norm{\boldsymbol{w^*}}\norm{\boldsymbol{w^{(T+1)}}}}
$$

from which the @eq:predictor-lineari-perceptron-teorema-tesi would automatically follow.

The proof is divided into two parts: first we will show that the numerator of the second member is greater than or equal to the numerator of the first member, and then we will show that the denominator of the second member is less than or equal to the denominator of the first member.


    - **First part (numerator)**: $\sprod{w^*}{w^{(T+1)}}\geqslant T$
    
    Let's rewrite the dot product through a summation as follows:

    $$
        \sprod{w^*}{w^{(T+1)}}=\sum_{t=1}^T\left(\sprod{w^*}{w^{(t+1)}}-\sprod{w^*}{w^{(t)}}\right)
    $$

    All the terms, in fact, will gradually cancel each other out, up to $t=T$, where only the first term of the difference will remain, which will not be canceled by any opposite.

    Applying the linearity property of the dot product we will write:

    $$
        \sum_{t=1}^T\left(\sprod{w^*}{w^{(t+1)}}-\sprod{w^*}{w^{(t)}}\right)=\sum_{t=1}^T\sprod{w^*}{w^{(t+1)}-w^{(t)}}
    $$

    According to the perceptron update rule:

    $$
        \boldsymbol{w^{(t+1)}}=\boldsymbol{w^{(t)}}+y_i\boldsymbol{x_i} \ \Longrightarrow \ \boldsymbol{w^{(t+1)}}-\boldsymbol{w^{(t)}}=y_i\boldsymbol{x_i}
    $$

    Returning to @eq:predictor-lineari-perceptron-teorema-dim-1 we will therefore write:

    $$
        \sprod{w^*}{w^{(T+1)}}=\sum_{t=1}^Ty_i\sprod{w^*}{x_i}
    $$

    From the definition of $\boldsymbol{w^*}$ given at the beginning of the proof, which is related to that of $B$ given among the hypotheses, it results:

    $$
        y_i\sprod{w^*}{x_i}\geqslant1 \ \Longrightarrow \ \sprod{w^*{w^{(T+1)}}\geqslant}\sum_{t=1}^T1=T
    $$

    - **Second part (denominator)**: $\norm{\boldsymbol{w^*}}\norm{\boldsymbol{w^{(T+1)}}}\leqslant\sqrt{T}RB$
    
    With the same reasoning used above for the first part of the proof, let's rewrite the squared norm of $\boldsymbol{w^{(T+1)}}$ through a summation:

    $$
        \norm{\boldsymbol{w^{(T+1)}}}^2=\sum_{t=1}^T\left(\norm{\boldsymbol{w^{(t+1)}}}^2-\norm{\boldsymbol{w^{(t)}}}^2\right)
    $$

    Let's make $\boldsymbol{w^{(t+1)}}$ explicit:
    
    \begin{align*}
        \norm{\boldsymbol{w^{(T+1)}}}^2&=\sum_{t=1}^T\left(\norm{\boldsymbol{w^{(t)}}+y_i\boldsymbol{x_i}}^2-\norm{\boldsymbol{w^{(t)}}}^2\right)=\\
        &=\sum_{t=1}^T\left(\cancel{\norm{\boldsymbol{w^{(t)}}}^2}+y_i^2\norm{\boldsymbol{x_i}}^2+2y_i\sprod{w^{(t)}}{x_i}-\cancel{\norm{\boldsymbol{w^{(t)}}}^2}\right)=\\
        &=\sum_{t=1}^T\left(\norm{\boldsymbol{x_i}}^2+2y_i\sprod{w^{(t)}}{x_i}\right)
    \end{align*}

    We will have that:


        - $\norm{\boldsymbol{x_i}}^2\leqslant R^2$ from the definition of $R$
        - $y_i\sprod{w^{(t)}}{x_i}\leqslant0$ because all the iterations of the algorithm up to the $T$-th one occur by virtue of the fact that the $i$-th point is not correctly classified
    

    Considering these upper bounds it follows:

    $$
        \norm{\boldsymbol{w^{(T+1)}}}^2\leqslant\sum_{t=1}^T\left(R^2+0\right)=TR^2 \ \iff \ \norm{\boldsymbol{w^{(T+1)}}}\leqslant\sqrt{T}R
    $$

    By definition $\norm{\boldsymbol{w^*}}=B$, so multiplying member by member:

    $$
        \norm{\boldsymbol{w^*}\norm{\boldsymbol{w^{(T+1)}}}\leqslant\sqrt{T}RB}
    $$



8.3.3 Problems with the Algorithm
The good news is that convergence for a linearly separable data set is guaranteed by the theorem just proved; the bad news is that the term \(B\) could grow exponentially with \(d\), that is, the dimension of the space, so for problems with high dimensional data convergence, although certain, could take too long.
The solutions in this case can be three:

Normalize the input vectors with respect to the largest among them, in order to reduce significant corrections of the weight vector due to the important difference in scale that can exist in the training data set. This action brings with it an inevitable reduction in the sensitivity of the model, which could be excessive when the difference in size of the considered vectors is too large.
Modify the order of the input vectors, since ordered in a certain way they could lead the weight vector in an initially “wrong” direction that takes time to be corrected.
Rearrange the problem in the form of a linear program, indicating the correct classification of the points as the constraints and choosing an arbitrary objective function to maximize or minimize.

Another element to take into consideration is that the perceptron does not provide a unique solution, but can provide different solutions based on the initial value of \(\boldsymbol{w}\).
A final - obvious - consideration to make concerns the case of non-realizability, that is, when the data set is not linearly separable. As we know, the perceptron is not able to arrive at a solution that correctly classifies all the points in the space, so a maximum number of iterations of the algorithm is fixed and at each iteration the number of misclassified points associated with the solution is saved: the one with the lowest number of mislabeled points is chosen as the solution as it is considered the best. This type of procedure is called the pocket algorithm, as you “pocket” the best solution among those found.


8.3.4 Example of Learning through the Perceptron
Before seeing a practical example of how the algorithm works, let’s introduce a last parameter called the learning rate \(\eta\): it is a real number, between \(0\) and \(1\), which is multiplied by \(y_i\boldsymbol{x_i}\) so that the term added to the correction of the weight vector is not so large.
The update will therefore be:
\[
    \boldsymbol{w^{(t+1)}} \ \longrightarrow \ \boldsymbol{w^{(t)}}+\eta y_i\boldsymbol{x_i}
\]
The learning rate is introduced so as not to have too large oscillations at each iteration, which would risk slowing down the convergence of the algorithm (in the case of realizability) or leading to suboptimal solutions (in the case of non-realizability): by limiting the oscillations, in fact, you have greater control over the update of the vector which should not change excessively if the number of misclassified points is low.
Let’s now start dealing with a specific example; let’s consider the following set of points: (The grid has a step of \(0.5\) both horizontally and vertically.)
Let’s fix the following parameters:
\[
    \eta=0.2 \ \ \text{and} \ \ \boldsymbol{w}=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0\\
        1\\
        0.5
    \end{pmatrix}
\]
Let’s calculate which halfspace it corresponds to:
\[
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0\\
        1\\
        0.5
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
        1 & x_1 & x_2
    \end{pmatrix}
    =0+x_1+0.5x_2=0 \ \Longrightarrow \ x_2=-\frac{1}{0.5}x_1=-2x_1
\]
Let’s visualize the halfspace in the graph:
Let’s start with the check of the classification of the data, starting from the first quadrant and proceeding clockwise, remembering that \(\sprod{w}{x}=x_1+0.5x_2\).

\(x_1=1\), \(x_2=1\), \(y=1\)
\[\begin{align*}
      &y\sprod{w}{x}=1+0.5\cdot1=1+0.5=1.5\geqslant0\\
      &y\sprod{w}{x}\geqslant0 \ \Longrightarrow \ \text{Correct classification}
  \end{align*}\]
\(x_1=1.5\), \(x_2=-0.5\), \(y=1\)
\[\begin{align*}
      &y\sprod{w}{x}=1.5+0.5\cdot(-0.5)=1.5-0.25=1.25\geqslant0\\
      &y\sprod{w}{x}\geqslant0 \ \Longrightarrow \ \text{Correct classification}
  \end{align*}\]
\(x_1=2\), \(x_2=-2\), \(y=-1\)
\[\begin{align*}
      &y\sprod{w}{x}=-[2+0.5\cdot(-2)]=-(2-1)=-1\leqslant0\\
      &y\sprod{w}{x}\leqslant0 \ \Longrightarrow \ \text{Wrong classification}
  \end{align*}\]

We have found a case of a misclassified point, so we update the weight vector according to the algorithm’s rule:
\[
    \boldsymbol{w} \ \longrightarrow \ \boldsymbol{w+\eta y\boldsymbol{x}=}
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0\\
        1\\
        0.5
    \end{pmatrix}
    +0.2\cdot(-1)
    \begin{pmatrix}
        1\\
        2\\
        -2
    \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0-0.2\\
        1-0.4\\
        0.5+0.4
    \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        -0.2\\
        0.6\\
        0.9
    \end{pmatrix}
\]
Let’s do the calculation again to visualize the line:
\[
    \begin{pmatrix}
        -0.2\\
        0.6\\
        0.9
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
        1 & x_1 & x_2
    \end{pmatrix}
    =-0.2+0.6x_1+0.9x_2=0 \ \Longrightarrow \ x_2=-\frac{0.6}{0.9}x_1+\frac{0.2}{0.9}
\]
I won’t repeat the calculations as it is clear from the graph that the three points are now correctly classified according to this new weight vector; moreover, the two points in the third quadrant are also classified correctly, while the last remaining point, the one in the second quadrant, is classified incorrectly. Let’s update the weight vector again according to the rule:
\[
    \boldsymbol{w} \ \longrightarrow \ \boldsymbol{w+\eta y\boldsymbol{x}=}
    \begin{pmatrix}
        -0.2\\
        0.6\\
        0.9
    \end{pmatrix}
    +0.2\cdot1
    \begin{pmatrix}
        1\\
        -2\\
        1
    \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        -0.2+0.2\\
        0.6-0.4\\
        0.9+0.2
    \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0\\
        0.2\\
        1.1
    \end{pmatrix}
\]
from which we find
\[
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0\\
        0.2\\
        1.1
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
        1 & x_1 & x_2
    \end{pmatrix}
    =0+0.2x_1+1.1x_2=0 \ \Longrightarrow \ x_2=-\frac{0.2}{1.1}x_1
\]
This solution gives us:
Unfortunately, a point that was previously correctly classified is no longer so, so we re-update the weight vector through its coordinates:
\[
    \boldsymbol{w} \ \longrightarrow \ \boldsymbol{w+\eta y\boldsymbol{x}=}
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0\\
        0.2\\
        1.1
    \end{pmatrix}
    +0.2\cdot1
    \begin{pmatrix}
        1\\
        1.5\\
        -0.5
    \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0+0.2\\
        0.2+0.3\\
        1.1-0.1
    \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0.2\\
        0.5\\
        1
    \end{pmatrix}
\]
\[
    \begin{pmatrix}
        0.2\\
        0.5\\
        1
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
        1 & x_1 & x_2
    \end{pmatrix}
    =0.2+0.5x_1+x_2=0 \ \Longrightarrow \ x_2=-0.5x_1-0.2
\]
This is the halfspace that gives us the correct classification of all the points in the set:

title: 8  Linear Predictors
text:
8.4 Linear Regression
Linear regression is an extremely common statistical tool for identifying the relationship that exists between some “explanatory” variables and a result expressed as a real number.
Suppose, for example, that we want to “predict” the price of a house in a certain city as a function of four parameters: the surface area, the number of rooms, the year of construction and the distance from the center. To this end, we could observe the real estate market to understand at what price houses are actually sold as a function of these parameters, trying to “quantify” the law that links the two things.
Formally, the “explanatory” variables will belong to a domain \(\mathcal{X}\in\mathbb{R}^d\), where \(d\) is the number of the aforementioned variables, while the result with a real value will be in the set of labels \(\mathcal{Y}\in\mathbb{R}\).
The predictor will correspond exactly to a linear function; the class to which it belongs, in fact, is
\[
    \mathcal{H}_{reg}=\left\{x\to\sprod{x'}{w'},\boldsymbol{w'}\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}\right\}
\]
which coincides exactly with the class of affine functions \(L_d\) (equation (eq:predictor-lineari-modello-delle-funzioni-affini-classe?)).
It remains to define the loss function and the algorithm useful for identifying the best predictor. As for the first, the quadratic objective function is often chosen, also called squared loss:
\[
    l(h(\boldsymbol{x}),y)=(h(\boldsymbol{x})-y)^2
\]
This function is very sensitive to so-called outliers, that is, to those points that are geometrically very distant from where the majority of them are located, which could therefore be the cause of overfitting. Depending on the available data set, in fact, one might prefer the mean absolute error, defined as the difference between \(h(\boldsymbol{x})\) and \(y\) in absolute value.
Finally, the empirical risk function to be minimized is none other than the mean squared error of the training set, that is, the average of the loss functions calculated for each point of \(\mathcal{S}\):
\[
    L_{\mathcal{S}}(h)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m\left(h\left(\boldsymbol{x_i}\right)-y_i\right)^2
\]


8.4.1 Quality of the Prediction
The average of the errors can be a good index to establish the quality of linear regression as a class of predictors useful for finding a correlation between the data. In figure (eq:predictor-lineari-regressione-lineare-correlazione?) we show four different “classifications” distinguished on the basis of the average error obtained:
\item[$@eq:predictor-lineari-regressione-lineare-correlazione-a$] The points are concentrated and follow a linear growth: this is the ideal condition for a linear regression, to which a very small error will thus be associated, demonstrating a strong correlation between the data
\item[$@eq:predictor-lineari-regressione-lineare-correlazione-b$] The correlation is weaker but the prediction is still good compared to the average: this translates into a high variance, often attributable to a random noise that partially alters the data collection and which must be taken into account in statistical analyses
\item[$@eq:predictor-lineari-regressione-lineare-correlazione-c$] There is no form of correlation, which mathematically translates into $E[Y|X]=E[Y]$, in the sense that the expected value is independent of the variable considered, so any line chosen will be equivalent to all the others, providing no information
\item[$@eq:predictor-lineari-regressione-lineare-correlazione-d$] The correlation is present and is also strong but it is not linear, so we are choosing the wrong class of hypotheses for this problem



8.4.2 Least Squares
Let’s now make the algorithm explicit to understand concretely how to identify the best predictor for a data set.
What we want to calculate is
\[
    \argmin_{\boldsymbol{w}}L_{\mathcal{S}}\left(h_{\boldsymbol{w}}\right)=\argmin_{\boldsymbol{w}}\left[\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\sprod{x_i}{w}-y_i\right)^2\right]
\]
since we want to minimize the empirical risk function.
Let’s then derive with respect to \(\boldsymbol{w}\) and set this derivative to zero:
\[
    \frac{2}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\sprod{x_i}{w}-y_i\right)\boldsymbol{x_i}=0 \ \Longrightarrow \ \sum_{i=1}^m\sprod{x_i}{w}\boldsymbol{x_i}=\sum_{i=1}^my_i\boldsymbol{x_i}
\]
We want to rewrite this expression in the form
\[
    A\boldsymbol{w}=\boldsymbol{b}
\]
so that it is simple to derive the weight vector.
The second member is trivial, since it is sufficient to set \(\boldsymbol{b}=\sum\limits_{i=1}^my_i\boldsymbol{x_i}\). As for the first member, let’s consider, for now, only the first term of the summation:
\[
    x_{11}w_1+x_{12}w_2+\dotsc+x_{1d}w_d
    \begin{pmatrix}
        x_{11}\\
        x_{12}\\
        \vdots\\
        x_{1d}
    \end{pmatrix}
    =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        x_{11}x_{11}w_1+x_{12}x_{11}w_2+\dotsc+x_{1d}x_{11}w_d\\
        x_{11}x_{12}w_1+x_{12}x_{12}w_2+\dotsc+x_{1d}x_{12}w_d\\
        \vdots\\
        x_{11}x_{1d}w_1+x_{12}x_{1d}w_2+\dotsc+x_{1d}x_{1d}w_d\\
    \end{pmatrix}
\]
We are interested in factoring out \(\boldsymbol{w}\), so we will have to define a matrix composed of \(d\) columns such that the product with \(\boldsymbol{w}\) returns the vector written above. It is clear that this matrix will be:
\[
    \begin{pmatrix}
        x_{11}x_{11} & x_{12}x_{11} & \dots & x_{1d}x_{11}\\
        x_{11}x_{12} & x_{12}x_{12} & \dots & x_{1d}x_{12}\\
        \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
        x_{11}x_{1d} & x_{12}x_{1d} & \dots & x_{1d}x_{1d}
    \end{pmatrix}
\]
which can also be rewritten as
\[
    \begin{pmatrix}
        x_{11}\\
        x_{12}\\
        \vdots\\
        x_{1d}
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
        x_{11} & x_{12} & \dots & x_{1d}
    \end{pmatrix}
    =\boldsymbol{x_1}\boldsymbol{x_1^T}
\]
Having to repeat this reasoning also for all the other \(m-1\) vectors, in the end we will obtain the matrix:
\[
    A=\sum_{i=1}^m\boldsymbol{x_i}\boldsymbol{x_i^T}=
    \begin{pmatrix}
        x_{11} & x_{21} & \dots & x_{m1}\\
        x_{12} & x_{22} & \dots & x_{m2}\\
        \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
        x_{1d} & x_{2d} & \dots & x_{md}
    \end{pmatrix}
    \begin{pmatrix}
        x_{11} & x_{12} & \dots & x_{1d}\\
        x_{21} & x_{22} & \dots & x_{2d}\\
        \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
        x_{m1} & x_{m2} & \dots & x_{md}
    \end{pmatrix}
\]
At this point, identifying the weight vector will be immediate:
\[
    A\boldsymbol{w}=\boldsymbol{b} \ \Longrightarrow \ \boxed{\boldsymbol{w}=A^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}}
\]

8.4.2.1 Closed-form Least Squares Solution

Let \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d}\) be the data matrix where each row is an example \(\boldsymbol{x}_i\), and \(\boldsymbol{y} \in \mathbb{R}^m\) be the vector of labels. The least squares problem is to minimize:
\[
{\mathcal{L}}(\boldsymbol{w}) = \|\boldsymbol{y} - X\boldsymbol{w}\|^2
\]
Taking the derivative with respect to \(\boldsymbol{w}\) and setting it to zero:
\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \boldsymbol{w}} = -2X^T(\boldsymbol{y} - X\boldsymbol{w}) = 0
\]
This yields the normal equations:
\[
X^T X \boldsymbol{w} = X^T \boldsymbol{y}
\]
The closed-form solution (when \(X^T X\) is invertible) is:
\[
\boldsymbol{w} = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T \boldsymbol{y}
\]
This is the optimal weight vector for linear regression with squared loss, and can be computed directly without iteration.




8.4.3 Polynomial Regression
If we want to perform a polynomial regression considering only one explanatory variable \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), we can exploit what we have seen so far for linear regression.
The generic polynomial of degree \(n\) will be given by
\[
    p(x)=a_0+a_1x+a_2x^2+\dotsc+a_nx^n
\]
which will automatically correspond to the predictor for our problem, so we will define the class of hypotheses as follows:
\[
    \mathcal{H}_{poly}^n=\{x\to p(x)\}
\]
It is useful to define a vector \(\boldsymbol{a}=\left(a_0,a_1,\dots,a_n\right)\) which must be multiplied by \((1,x,\dots,x^n)\) in order to return \(p(x)\). We recall that \(x\) represents the data of the learning set, so formally we define a function \(\psi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\) such that
\[
    \psi(x)=(1,x,\dots,x^n)
\]
The dot product sought is
\[
    p(x)=\left\langle\psi(x),\boldsymbol{a}\right\rangle
\]
from which we deduce that the class of hypotheses coincides with that of linear regression (equation (eq:predictor-lineari-regressione-lineare-classe-di-hypotesis?)).
By deriving the vector of coefficients \(\boldsymbol{a}\) through linear regression (with the least squares method), we will find the polynomial of degree \(n\) that best fits the available data.
An element to take into consideration is that, in this case, the variables multiplied by the coefficients are not independent, since it is the same data raised to a different power: this means that if there is some form of noise in the sampling, this is propagated and amplified along the vector \(\psi(x)\).

title: 8  Linear Predictors
text:
8.5 Logistic Regression
With logistic regression we are able to solve classification problems through the use of regression.
It arises from the problem of the separability of a set: we could say that algorithms that provide for a binary classification - such as the perceptron - do not admit “exceptions”, in the sense that the solution is considered correct only when there is no misclassified element.
